with_skill.expectation: Does not name a reporting line before the funded driver is identified and attributed to a named leader.

Asks explicitly why the company funds developer relations, offering driver options such as developer adoption, sales enablement, developer enablement, product input, ecosystem, contributor community or employer brand.
Quotes the reporting-line spread with the survey year attached (marketing around 33%, product around 22%, CEO around 20%, engineering around 20%, sales around 3%).
Names what an engineering line starves (narrative, measurement literacy or budget defence) and its characteristic failure of the team being used as overflow engineering capacity.
Asks what is politically fixed - a line that cannot move, or a manager who cannot be moved.
Requires a work inventory listing each recurring surface with a named owner, that owner's manager, hours per week, and what breaks if the surface stops, before proposing any structure.
Records a named person as owner today for each surface, plus that person's manager.
Marks each surface as owned, shared, unowned, or informally absorbed by someone with a different job title.
Labels the 70% ceiling as a chosen, adjustable baseline rather than an industry standard or benchmark.
Requires one accountable owner plus one named backup per surface, and flags any surface at a bus factor of one as a risk.
Rejects hub-and-spoke at this headcount rather than shrinking it to fit.
States the hub-and-spoke staffing floor: a hub of two to three plus at least two spokes, a management layer and a standing forum.
Notes hub-and-spoke takes about a quarter to stand up and a quarter to unwind.
Recommends centralized as the only candidate shape under roughly ten full-time people.
Labels the ten-person threshold as this skill's own chosen baseline, not a published finding.
Cites that around 69% of surveyed teams are under ten people, with the year attached.
Applies the scaling test: further investment must increase output more than it increases input.
Warns that a hub that approves work rather than enables it becomes a bottleneck wearing a standards label.
States that the near board date pushes the choice toward centralized, which is reversible in about a week and adds near-zero coordination.
Names the shared craft and the shared calendar as what embedded costs.
States that embedded's coordination is a standing job rather than a one-off setup cost.
Gives the embedded staffing floor as one advocate per host team plus a craft owner somewhere, i.e. at least five advocates plus a craft owner for five squads.
Produces interlock lines and a named arbiter rather than recommending the merge as the first move.
Assigns exactly one interaction mode to the docs / technical-writing team.
Names the mode as one of collaboration, X-as-a-service or facilitation, and attributes the model to Team Topologies.
Names X-as-a-service as the default mode for docs drafts, reviews and structure decisions.
States that more than one mode per adjacent team means nobody can say where the boundary is.
Cites that technical writing is staffed on around 42.7% of surveyed teams, with the year attached, and sits under another manager in most of the rest.
States that collaboration mode needs an end date or the team silently becomes interrupt-driven.
Warns against reorganising when the real fix is declaring ownership and re-scoping.
Records technical writing on the six-function coverage map as owned by another named team or shared with a named split, in writing.
Names an arbiter for the sales interlock.
Adds a re-org trigger tied to that interlock breaching its cap or staying in collaboration mode past its end.
Keeps compensation out of the org design brief entirely rather than including it with a caveat.
Names the function the team moves to when it crosses a stated size threshold.
States which career ladder the role sits on - engineering, marketing, or a developer-relations-specific one.
Warns that a borrowed ladder promotes against criteria that do not describe the work, which leaks retention slowly rather than failing loudly.
States explicitly that it is in brainstorming mode before recommending anything.
States the weekly coordination each candidate adds and what undoing it would take.
Orders the candidates by efficiency - value per unit of effort - and says the ordering out loud rather than implying it by row order.
Leaves the choice to the accountable person before detailing anything below the recommendation.
Presents the brief one section at a time and seeks agreement before writing the next section.
Names the shared-voice problem a split creates: two teams, one audience, two calendars, two metric sets.
Names the one-re-org-per-new-leader pattern and prices each redraw at roughly a quarter of rebuilding interlocks.
Requires planned work to fit inside 70% of stated capacity and says that ceiling is a chosen baseline.
Ranks the individual-developer and enterprise audiences for this horizon instead of splitting effort evenly between them.
States that consumer-marketing org patterns do not transfer, because a developer audience evaluates the artefact rather than the campaign.
Applies the awareness / enablement / engagement split across advocates, developer experience and community management, attributed to Mary Thengvall.
